# Design a Project-to-Contractor Matching System

> **▶ [Solve it on TrueInterview](https://trueinterview.io/questions/design-a-project-to-contractor-matching-system)** — free, no card: the interview workspace, an AI interviewer to push back on your design, and the reference solution.

## Problem

Design a two-sided platform that connects posted work opportunities with independent contractors. Discuss the most important data-modeling and product tradeoffs, how candidate lists are produced and ordered, and how the system can learn from observed results without amplifying the exposure patterns that already exist in historical data.

### Constraints and assumptions

- Each project describes the required skills, timing, workload, location or time-zone restrictions, and budget.
- Each contractor describes their skills, availability, preferences, rate, and eligibility to work.
- A contractor may qualify for many projects but has finite capacity for simultaneous work.
- Both parties need explanations for recommendations and may reject a suggested match.
- New projects and contractors usually have very little behavioral history.

### Clarifying questions to explore

- Does the product return a ranked list, assign work automatically, or support mutual choice?
- Which constraints are strictly non-negotiable?
- What outcome counts as a successful match, and when is that outcome observed?
- How much do fairness, diversity, and exploration matter for the product?

## Part 1: Requirements and data model

Separate absolute eligibility rules from softer preferences, and define the core entities: projects, contractors, availability, interactions, and outcomes.

This section should address:

- Hard eligibility checks versus soft preference signals
- Time-varying availability and limited concurrent capacity
- A trustworthy skill taxonomy with evidence of proficiency
- Consent, privacy, and explainability requirements

## Part 2: Retrieval and ranking

Design candidate generation, scoring, cold-start behavior, and a mechanism for mutual acceptance.

This section should address:

- High-recall retrieval that runs before expensive ranking
- Constraint-aware scoring and calibration
- Exploration for brand-new projects and contractors
- Capacity constraints and two-sided marketplace effects

## Part 3: Evaluation and operations

Define offline and online metrics, feedback loops, failure handling, and monitoring for bias or opportunity concentration.

This section should address:

- Match quality beyond simple click engagement
- Counterfactual or randomized evaluation methods
- Exposure and acceptance funnels
- Drift, abuse, and unfair-allocation detection

### Follow-up questions

1. How would you stop a small number of highly popular contractors from receiving nearly all opportunities?
2. How can the system learn when contractors can only accept or reject matches that were shown to them?
3. What should happen when no available contractor satisfies every hard constraint?

## Hints

<details>
<summary>Hint 1</summary>

Treat matching as a two-sided ranking problem where both project-to-contractor and contractor-to-project views matter, not a single global score.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Hint 2</summary>

Use a candidate-generation step (skill/availability/location filters or embeddings) followed by a learned ranking model over features from both sides.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Hint 3</summary>

Watch the feedback-loop edge case: training only on past matches amplifies existing exposure bias, so plan for exploration, propensity weighting, or randomized logging.

</details>
